new_statements.quote: 2.3 Stress. The majority of words in Nggem are stressed on the penultimate syllable. However there are some exceptions to this, indicating that stress is phonemic. No minimal pairs have been found, but the following examples illustrate varying positions in which stress can fall. Examples (18a) and (18b) are from Rule (1975:15). 18) a. /ˈaɓi/ abi 'nose' b. /aɓís/ abis 'mouth' c. /apúla/ avula 'pregnant' d. /ˈapulak/ avulak 'clatter'. Stress is not written in the orthography, and it is not recorded in later chapters unless the discussion of a particular feature warrants it. [p. 119:] When compounded with a personal object auxiliary, the primary verb root still receives independent word stress - that is, the penultimate syllable is stressed, as is that of the object auxiliary

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (language not in catalog, no existing statements). First statement: penultimate stress as the majority pattern, with unpredictable exceptions the author calls phonemic.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable in the majority of Nggem words (disyllables in the phonology chapter are all marked initial = penult: ákwa, húnggwa, ládya, ánye, móga, ísok; trisyllabic apyárat, avúla penult). A minority of words carry stress elsewhere (final abís 'mouth', antepenultimate ávulak 'clatter'), which the author takes as evidence that stress is phonemic, though he found no minimal pairs. Stress is not marked in the orthography. In verb + object-auxiliary compounds each member keeps its own penultimate stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; p. 119 says that in primary-verb + personal-object-auxiliary compounds both the verb root and the auxiliary carry their own (penultimate) word stress, i.e. two stresses in what speakers write as one word.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions to penult: /aɓís/ 'mouth' (final), /ˈapulak/ 'clatter' (antepenult) (18a-b from Rule 1975:15); no minimal pairs. Morphological: the orientation suffix -nak (ORIENT) is itself stressed (p. 57, so final stress on those adjectives); the future portmanteau -yogon/-sogon is never stressed, stress falls on the preceding syllable (e.g. nu-yogon, p. 99). Stress conditions allophony: palatalisation of n, d, m, nd, s, ngg, k, t after a stressed syllable with i (p. 17); a -> e raising in an unstressed syllable before a stressed syllable with an alveolar + a (p. 22). No mention of tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Describes the 'Eastern' dialect of Nggem (19 of the 22 Nggem villages, Kobakma and Kelila districts, Jayawijaya regency, Papua, Indonesia); the 'Western' dialect of the three westernmost villages (90% cognate, closer to Western Dani) is not described (p. 7). Two of the four stress examples (18a-b) are cited from Rule (1975:15), an earlier unpublished statement of the Nggem language of Kobakma.

The PDF is openly hosted but an automated-access block Turnstile blocks automated downloads by automated download; a person opening the URL in a normal browser, or a Harvard-affiliated download via ProQuest (the Harvard library catalogue), should get it in one click.

sources.note: Title and second-hand description only. It is a first-hand phonemic statement of Nggem that includes stress-marked forms (Etherington takes examples of non-penultimate stress from its p. 15); whether it comments on tone/pitch is not established.3 Stress (penultimate with lexical exceptions) plus 'rising intonation' on questions - so if any first-hand remark on Nggem tone exists, this 1975 statement is the only other place it could be.
